title: Saving for Retirement
objective: After this level you can explain why starting early matters so much when saving for retirement.
summary: Time does most of the work in retirement saving: the earlier you start, the longer growth earns growth. Pensions promise a benefit; in 401(k)-style plans, the worker carries the risk.

cards.headline: Skip a $1 candy bar every day for a year. What is that $365 worth in 30 years?
cards.body: The US Securities and Exchange Commission ran the numbers. Save the $365 once, let it earn 5% a year, and it grows to $465.84 in five years. Leave it alone for 30 years and it becomes $1,577.50. Same candy bars, very different payoff.

cards.headline: Time does the heavy lifting
cards.body: Look closer. In its first five years, the $365 earns about $101. In the next 25, about $1,112. Same money, same rate: the difference is time, because growth keeps earning growth of its own. That's why the SEC's guide for people starting their first job says starting early is key: the younger you are when you begin, the more time your investments have to grow.

mascot.line: Your future self will thank you. Possibly with a candy bar.

cards.headline: Who carries the risk?
cards.body: Many people save through work. A traditional pension is the employer's promise: it invests the money and pays you a benefit based on your pay and years of service. In a 401(k)-style plan, the account is yours: you choose how much to save and how it's invested, and some employers add a match, such as 50 cents per dollar. As savings moved to 401(k)s, the risk moved from employers to workers. Level 36's Enron staff found out what that means.

learned: Starting early gives money more time to grow
Growth earns growth, so later years add the most
401(k)-style plans put the risk on the worker

questions.prompt: In the SEC's candy-bar example, what turns $365 into $1,577.50?

options.label: Adding $365 more every single year
options.rationale: The $365 is saved once, then left alone.

options.label: Buying a candy company's shares
options.rationale: It's just savings earning 5% a year.

options.label: Thirty years of growth at 5% a year

questions.explanation: Saved once and earning 5% a year, the $365 grows to $465.84 in five years and $1,577.50 in 30.

questions.prompt: In the example, the $365 earns about $101 in five years but about $1,112 over the next 25. Why?

options.label: The interest rate rises in later years
Growth keeps earning growth, so time matters most
The saver adds more money every year
options.rationale: Nothing is added after the first $365.

options.label: Banks pay a bonus to long-term savers
options.rationale: No bonus: just time and a steady rate.

questions.explanation: Each year the growth itself starts growing, so the later years add far more. Starting early buys more of those years.

questions.prompt: Level 36's Enron workers held their 401(k)s in company stock. In a 401(k)-style plan, who carries the investment risk?

options.label: The employer
options.rationale: That's a traditional pension, where the employer promises the benefit.

options.label: The government
options.rationale: A 401(k) is the worker's own account.

options.label: The stock exchange
options.rationale: Exchanges match trades; they carry none of your risk.

questions.explanation: In a 401(k) the worker chooses and owns the investments, so the risk moved from employers to workers.
